When a condition says that one point lies near another,
write it as membership in a [ball](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/vector-calculus.html#def-ball):
$\vx \in \ball{\vx^*}{\tolin}$,
read "$\vx$ is in the ball of radius $\tolin$ around $\vx^*$".
Do not write it as an inequality on the distance between the two points.

Ezra Morrison asked for the rule on 2026-11-20,
after rewriting the [local maximizer](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/optimization-critical-points.html#def-local-maximizer) definition in mds:

> should we add a psw principle for writing this type of relationship using balls rather than inequalities?

Ball notation is easier to read for three reasons:

- It says what the condition means, "near $\vx^*$",
  instead of a computation that the reader must interpret.
- It names the set,
  so the same symbol can serve as the set that a [quantifier](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/chapters/predicates-quantifiers.html#def-quantifier) runs over,
  the [domain](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/functions.html#def-domain) of a function,
  or a set to compare with another.
- It extends the [double inequality](#def-double-inequality) rule.
  On the real line,
  a ball is an open interval,
  and $x \in \ball{c}{\tolin}$ says the same as $x \in (c - \tolin, c + \tolin)$.

::: {#exm-ball-neighborhood}

## Rewriting a neighborhood condition

<!-- check-ball-neighborhoods: allow: the counter-example shows the inequality form on purpose -->
> ❌ $f(\vx^*) \ge f(\vx)$ for every $\vx$ with $\norm{\vx - \vx^*} < \tolin$.
>
> ✅ $f(\vx^*) \ge f(\vx)$ for every $\vx \in \ball{\vx^*}{\tolin}$.

The ✅ version quantifies over a set,
so the reader sees at once that the condition is about the points near $\vx^*$.

:::

Keep the inequality when the distance itself is the point,
as in these cases:

- the [definition of the ball](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/vector-calculus.html#def-ball);
- the [triangle inequality](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-inner-products.html#thm-triangle-inequality);
- a bound on how far an estimate lies from its target;
- a stopping rule for an algorithm.
